anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Static mismatch between table/partition layout, index set, data types, and the workload’s access patterns, forcing otherwise well-written queries into inefficient scans or lookups.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level memory, I/O, parallelism, or background-worker settings that are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, causing bottlenecks or wasted resources even when the underlying components are healthy.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside heap pages or index structures that makes persisted data and index entries unreliable or unusable.

When these three root causes coexist, symptoms overlap and intensify: queries that already suffer from missing or non-covering indexes choose full scans that are further slowed by mis-sized buffer pools or aggressive checkpoint storms, while corrupted pages or mis-linked index leaves cause unpredictable row omissions, duplicates, or engine errors. Operators may observe alternating patterns of plan regressions, sudden I/O bursts, fluctuating CPU spin on lightweight locks, rising retry or deadlock rates during maintenance tasks, and intermittent corruption warnings. Autovacuum, consistency-check, or index-rebuild operations may stall because configuration limits starve them of memory or I/O quota, yet their failure leaves structural damage uncorrected, feeding back into even costlier scan plans. Overall performance and correctness become erratic, and separating design flaws from runtime mis-tuning or corruption side effects becomes extremely difficult.

Causally, a poor schema and index design inflates table and index footprints, increasing buffer-pool and checkpoint pressure; if memory and I/O parameters are already mis-tuned, the engine is forced into more frequent flushes and page evictions, amplifying latency spikes. Vigorous churn from inefficient queries and oversized structures lengthens maintenance windows, raising the likelihood of interrupted writes or partial rebuilds that introduce on-disk corruption. Conversely, latent data-block or index damage can mask the benefits of any later design improvements and lead DBAs to over-allocate memory or alter checkpoint settings in futile attempts to recover performance, deepening the configuration mismatch. The intertwined feedback loop between static design flaws, dynamic mis-configuration, and lurking physical corruption drives the database into a degraded and unstable state that affects both transactional and analytical workloads.

entry.official_definition: Specifies how long transmitted data may remain unacknowledged before the TCP connection is forcibly closed.
entry.trigger_condition: TCP data sent by PostgreSQL remains unacknowledged longer than tcp_user_timeout on systems supporting TCP_USER_TIMEOUT.
entry.workload_impact: The TCP connection is forcibly closed.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
